169.t: Writing for Bailey; Leonard Gay's band at the Cotton Clubs
169.s: He writes for a tenor player named Bailey, then joins Leonard Gay's eight-piece band at the Cotton Club in Milwaukee and Cincinnati.
169.q: They just get paid, you know. I said, 'Well, what the fuck happens to me?' I'm here and I can't stay with this group, and have nothing happen. So I started writing for a cat named Bailey. He had a sextet.

169.s: Pianist Step Wharton calls him for his big band, which McGhee ranks as the best he had played in, until it breaks up for lack of gigs.
169.q: Yeah, or '39. No, wait a minute. We went to Cincinnati to the Cotton Club, right? Then we went back up to Superior, Wisconsin for six months, and then we came back and then I joined Step. So that would make it about '39 or '40, the early part of '40 maybe. Yeah, I think it was the early part of…

169.t: Jimmy Rochelle's band with Milt Buckner and Wardell Gray
169.s: In Michigan he joins Jimmy Rochelle, a dance band with good soloists including Milt Buckner and Wardell Gray, and compares it with Gay and Wharton.
169.q: Yeah, I think it was about the best band. No, Step Wharton's band was the best band, but Jimmy's band wasn't bad, because with Milt Buckner and Wardell...

91.t: Billy Page's band to Pittsburgh, Earl Hines and the Eldridges
91.s: In 1925 Carter replaced the altoist in Billy Page's band, went to Pittsburgh, and played with Earl Hines's sextet and the Eldridge brothers.
91.q: In 1925, there was a band that came to New York called the Broadway Syncopators -- that was Billy Page -- and they played at a place called the Capitol -- it was Capitol something, but it was a big cabaret in New York, a nightclub, and I think they had a saxophone player

91.s: Horace Henderson's band from Wilberforce invited him to join after a few gigs; he toured with them.
91.q: I know that there had been -- I'm trying to think -- I think I played a couple of gigs around there with them. Was it in Pittsburgh, or around Pittsburgh? In the area, though. Following which, he

566.t: The boys go north; her 1934 visit to Buffalo and first singing at the Spiderweb
566.s: The school band members left Louisville for Cleveland and Buffalo. Just out of high school, she visited Luke Stewart and his wife in Buffalo and was pushed to sing at the Spiderweb with Al Sears's band, her first New York State appearance with a microphone.
566.ch: Central High, first records and leaving home
566.q: Yeah. And then they came to Buffalo and I was out of school then and I came to Buffalo to visit, who was that? The best guitar player I . . .

566.t: Back to Louisville, then the Cotton Club in Cincinnati with Al Sears's band
566.s: Homesick after Albany, she went home and then took a job at the Cotton Club in a Cincinnati hotel. Her band there was Al Sears's, whom she knew from Buffalo, with pianist Bugs Roberts from Kentucky.
566.q: Yes, I guess. And so I went back on home and as soon as I got home I had to call the man that owned the Club in Cincinnati and he wanted me to come up and let him hear me. So my mother, father and I, we drove up one Sunday. And it turned out the man had me.

389.t: Bob-Lo boats and the band that became Casa Loma
389.s: While Goldkette was away, Challis wrote for a Detroit band playing the Bob-Lo boats that later became the Casa Loma orchestra.
389.ch: Detroit 1927: Pollack, Casa Loma, Atlantic City
389.q: But in those days, some of those tunes could go for a year, year and a half, two years without -- no problem whatever. Well, anyway, I didn't get out on the road at all with them and it seemed like there were no tunes required for the trip and I was asked to, by a guy in the office there if I…

389.t: Russ Morgan, Charlie Horvath and a first arrangement for Goldkette
389.s: Russ Morgan took him to meet manager Charlie Horvath, who asked for a trial arrangement; Challis explains the Goldkette bands around Detroit.
389.q: Now, let me see, well, I went up one Sunday. We had Sunday off and they were working on Sunday in Detroit, it didn't make any difference. I think Monday was the night they had off, so I went down there and little old home week. Talking to Russ and Fuzzy and Itzy, they were in the band, and I met…

529.t: Moving to Miami to the Entertainers Club and Frank Brown's band
529.s: With Johnny Burdine he moves to Miami to work with Rubin Mitchell at the Entertainers Club, where Frank Brown's big band plays; Ridley clarifies the timeline.
529.q: So I stayed home and I continued playing with the Charley Brantley's band. So we got another piano player from--a boy came from Detroit. And so I--we played with that band until we got tired of that. And Johnny Burdine and myself, we decided to move on down to Miami, you know. Big time lifetime…

529.t: The big bands that passed through Florida, Snookum Russell and Roy Haynes
529.s: Sam recalls the many big bands, Carolina Cottonpickers and Louis Russell's band where he met Ray Brown and Roy Haynes.
529.ch: Race, critics and the big bands
529.q: And it was traveling all over the country. There were a lot of bands in and out man. So there was a lot of work, for a lot of musicians man, you know. Jesus Christ, I remember those bands used to come through my home, man.

862.t: Arriving in New Orleans in 1913 and joining the Excelsior
862.s: Arriving in 1913, he had trouble getting hired because he could not read or play by head, then joined the Excelsior as a regular.
862.ch: Brass bands and coming to New Orleans
862.q: After they found us, you understand what kind of man I was, I couldn't, the rest, I couldn't. They didn't think they'd come and knock them to do.

662.s: Straight out of high school she was recommended as pianist and auditioned on orchestrations such as Alabama Bound. Her mother let her go.
662.q: One of my friends over here heard that they wanted a pianist. And he recommended me. And they came over and interviewed me. And that's where it started.

251.t: First stop Dallas and joining Troy Floyd's band
251.s: After leaving New Orleans with a banjo player and others he played a Dallas honky-tonk, met Lee Collins, and got Claude Kennedy's chair in Troy Floyd's band.
251.ch: Leaving New Orleans and Troy Floyd
251.q: He was one of the masters. So I said, yeah, I can play something else. So I started out and I tried to improvise one of the three I was playing. He says, that's the same one you've been playing all the time. But in volume it all, huh? He says, that's the same one. Right on the truck then. Yeah,…

288.t: Arriving in New Orleans in 1909 and joining the Silver Leaf band in 1913
288.s: He studied for two years, worked at a seed company, joined the Silver Leaf band, then formed Maple Leaf and his own band.
288.ch: Vidals, blues, teachers and the Silver Leaf band
288.q: I didn't know them then, you see. Oh, you didn't know their names? No, because I was living on Esplanade and Dupre. And I was working at Steckler Seed Company, see, but I was working in the yard then. And every now and then I'd go out and listen to the band playing. But I was taking music lessons…

572.t: Photo of Jules Bauduc's 1928 band; Ray leaves New Orleans in 1926
572.s: The interviewer reads the names on a 1928 photo of Jules's band; Bauduc says he left in 1926 with Johnny Bayersdorffer and the Scranton Sirens.
572.ch: Jules's band and the move north
572.q: left left left to go up north. That was about 1926. That's when johnny well and it was I was still with johnny I was still with Johnny Beisdolph and we collaborated with Billy Lustig and made it for Scranton Sirens and went to Chicago, see? Well, at the finish of the Chicago job at the Rendezvous,…

798.t: Never a dance band; moving to the Eureka band after the Tonic Triad
798.s: Clark says he never played dance bands and joined the Eureka Band around 1931-32 after the Tonic Triad broke up.
798.q: No, not at that time. After this band broke up, then that's when I came into the Urica Band.

673.t: Cooper with Nat Towles, 1949, first snow
673.s: They find they shared Vic Schrader's agency; Cooper joined Nat Towles in 1949 and first saw snow.
673.q: Oh, sure. He worked out of the same office we worked out of, Vic Schrader’s.

420.t: Roomful of Blues near-miss, Scott's band and Widespread Depression
420.s: He nearly joined Roomful of Blues, ended up in Scott Hamilton's band briefly, then went with Chuck Riggs to Widespread Depression in Vermont to save for New York.
420.q: This would have been ‘75 I guess. So I went down to Providence and hung out on the scene with Hamilton a lot. Chris Flory had a quartet, because Scott already had his own band, with a great guitar player by the name of Fred Bates. And with Chuck Riggs as well, who followed him on into New York and…

326.t: Tommy Reynolds, Bob Strong, Frankie Carle and Jan Savitt bands
326.s: Meets Tommy Reynolds' band at the beach, drops out of school for Bob Strong's New York trip, then Frankie Carle and Jan Savitt, finishing high school in Hollywood.
326.q: it was. So we went up there and a big band came through there that was looking for a trombone player, and so this was in the summertime, a band by the name of Tommy Reynolds, and he was from New York. He was one of the up-and-coming new bands and they were going into the Lincoln Hotel in New York I…

415.t: Joining Buddy Morrow's Tommy Dorsey ghost band
415.s: Invited to join at a Cleveland festival, two and a half years on the road, bus life, and the spotlight Morrow gave him.
415.ch: Dorsey band and moving to New York
415.q: It’s kind of a two part thing. When I was living in Cleveland and I was playing of course in this polka band, and at the same time I started branching out and playing with jazz groups around town. Flash forward a few years, I’m in college. I get called to play at a jazz festival in Cleveland with…

824.t: Joining the Goldkette band in 1925 to replace Tommy Dorsey
824.s: Trumpeter Freddy Ferrar hears Willcox at Owasco Lake and recruits him to Goldkette; Willcox leaves the California Ramblers, arrives at the Graystone in Detroit and meets Bix and Trumbauer.
824.q: Yeah, exactly. That’s the guy that I replaced with the Goldkette band. It happened in 1925. If you’ve got time for it, this was a big point in my life. I was playing in Auburn, New York. And I was playing all summer at Owasco Lake at the head of the lake, a lakeside park. And we were coming to the…

85.t: Horace Henderson and the Wilberforce Collegians; elected leader
85.s: Horace invited him to join the Wilberforce band; touring, the Club Bamville job, and the band electing Carter leader.
85.q: I met with Horace Henderson in Pittsburgh. He came there to play. Oh, did I play with him one night? I don’t even remember. But he invited me to come join the orchestra. He thought it might even be a good opportunity for me to go to school if I was so inclined, but, of course, I couldn’t have…

86.t: Cleveland with remnants of the Alphonso Trent band
86.s: Edison explains he never played with Trent but with the band's former members in Cleveland, where he met Roy Eldridge and other young players.
86.ch: Road tales, then Cleveland, St. Louis and Harlem
86.q: Yeah, I did. I went there with a band that was formerly Alphonso Trent Band. It has been quoted that I played with Alphonso Trent but I never did. He had taken ill up in New Hampshire and they took him back to Fort Smith, AR, and some of the guys kept the band together. So, they came to Columbus,…

134.t: King Kolax recruits Gene Ammons; Freeman stays in school
134.s: Kolax came to DuSable for the two tenor hotshots; Jug left, and Freeman stayed to finish school.
134.ch: Chicago repertoire, bands and the end of the big-band era
134.q: No. Kolax come along about the same time as Earl Hines, because when Earl Hines left the Grand Terrace, Kolax went in with his big band.

371.t: The Three Sixes in Detroit, Teddy Buckner, and the Cotton Club
371.s: The Three Sixes big band led by Teddy Buckner, Snooky Young's presence at the Cincinnati Cotton Club.
371.ch: Early bands and the road to New York
371.q: That was in Detroit. That was in Detroit on Adams Street. Now that was a big band. Glitzy, the leader of it was a saxophone player who is the brother of a pianist. He played block chords. He was the one that originated the block chord structure.

225.t: Clarence Love, Snookum Russell and Fats Navarro
225.s: Johnson recalls his first pro bands, rooming with Fats Navarro in Snookum Russell's band, and the next job with Benny Carter.
225.q: I’m trying to remember whether it was Clarence Love. It was probably Clarence Love, which came before Snookum Russell. That would be about right.

409.t: Staying with Eagle Eye, then Alonzo Ross with Edmond Hall
409.s: Cootie stayed with Eagle Eye for a while before moving with Hall to Alonzo Ross's band.
409.ch: First bands and the road in the South
409.q: Yeah. Then I stayed with the band, with Eagle Eye, for quite awhile. I don't know exactly how many years. Then I went with Alonzo Ross's band. He was from Florida, too.

147.t: Jimmy Lunceford, the athletic instructor who formed the band
147.s: Crawford describes Lunceford's Fisk and Columbia background, his return to Memphis, and the band's summers at Lakeside and move north to Cleveland.
147.ch: Memphis boyhood and the Ohio territory years
147.q: Now, I started out, as I forestated, with an orchestra leader (inaudible). He was an athletic instructor there, Jimmy Lunsford. He finished Fisk University, and then he came to New York. Pardon me. He took up postgraduate work at Columbia University, and also he tried to join Fletcher Henderson's…

235.t: Goofus Carnell, Idlewilde and meeting Thad and Hank Jones
235.s: He met Thad and Hank Jones in Pontiac and Goofus Carnell put a band together for a summer at Idlewilde.
235.ch: First jobs and finding his sound
235.q: When I look back, I don't know how this happened...Oh, oh yes I do know how it happened. I met...after I got started playin' pretty good... I met Thad Jones and Hank Jones in Pontiac which was 30 or 35 miles from my home. Goofus Carnell...now it all comes back to me...Goofus Carnell, he took us…

168.t: Joining Peanuts Holland's group in Buffalo and its repertoire, 1935
168.s: A bandleader passing through Boston called him to Buffalo, where he joined Peanuts Holland's small group for about six months, playing Ellington-era standards.
168.ch: Boston, Buffalo and finding a style
168.q: through Boston while I was there, and he said he liked the way I played, you know, and said that, if he ever needed a bass player, he's going to call on me, you know, and I would be coming that way or going back home. I told him I was going back home very soon after that time, but maybe I would…
